restatements.text: Names the measure the Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026.
Declares findings that Californians face high costs of living and taxes, and asserts that taxing retirement holdings, personal savings, or retroactively applying taxes would be harmful and unfair.
States the measure's purpose is to protect residents' ability to save by prohibiting new taxes on personal property and retirement assets, and requiring new taxes to apply only prospectively.
Adds Article VIII to the California Constitution.

Prohibits the state from enacting any new tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, or personal savings on or after January 1, 2026. Exempts taxes that were already in effect and collected by the end of 2025, as well as existing real property taxes.

Prohibits the state from enacting new retroactive taxes based on conduct, activities, or residency status prior to the tax's effective date. Provides an exception allowing the Legislature to pass a retroactive tax going back no more than 365 days if the Governor declares an emergency or fiscal emergency and the tax revenues are strictly limited to responding to it.

Defines retirement holdings and personal savings to include pensions, 401(k)s, mutual funds, and all personal property, including financial assets, business interests, digital assets, and personal belongings used for financial planning.
Applies the provisions to all statewide initiative measures on the ballot on or after January 1, 2026.

Declares that any other initiative on the same ballot establishing a tax on personal savings or a retroactive tax is in conflict, and if this measure receives more votes, the conflicting measure is void.
Includes a severability clause ensuring that if any part of the act is struck down, the rest remains in effect.
Specifies that the act takes effect and becomes operative at the earliest possible date allowed by the Constitution.
Requires the act to be construed liberally to achieve its purposes.

Mandates the Attorney General to appoint independent counsel to defend the act if the Governor and Attorney General refuse to do so. Creates a continuous appropriation from the General Fund to pay for the independent counsel's costs.

evidence.why: It removes the government's power to enact a tax on the ownership of personal property.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. The measure would add Article VIII to the state Constitution to prohibit the state from imposing any new tax on the ownership or control of personal property, retirement holdings, and individually-owned assets. It would also prohibit the state from enacting new taxes that operate retroactively based on past conduct or residency, with limited exceptions for emergency taxes applying retroactively up to 365 days.

The measure makes a continuous appropriation from the General Fund to pay for independent counsel if the Governor and Attorney General decline to defend the measure against legal challenges. It also carries an opportunity cost by permanently removing the state's ability to raise revenue through wealth taxes or retroactive taxes, restricting future budget options.

Taxpayers, particularly those with significant personal property, business interests, and retirement accounts, benefit by being shielded from potential future wealth or asset taxes. The state government loses the ability to implement these types of taxes, and the broader public might bear the cost if alternative, broader taxes are used to raise revenue instead, or if services are reduced due to lack of revenue. Independent attorneys could benefit from state-funded contracts to defend the measure.

By preventing wealth taxes and retroactive taxes, the measure may encourage individuals to accumulate and keep assets in California rather than relocating. It may also incentivize the legislature to find alternative ways to structure taxes (such as increasing income or sales taxes) to raise revenue without triggering the prohibition.

The measure asserts that Californians face a high cost of living and high taxes, and that taxing retirement savings or applying taxes retroactively undermines financial planning. The mechanism—a constitutional ban on wealth taxes and retroactive taxes—directly prevents the state from enacting such policies. If wealth taxes or retroactive taxes were proposed to address inequality or sudden revenue shortfalls, the measure would prevent those specific tools from being used.

Independent counsel appointed under the measure would gain discretion and state funding to defend the law if elected officials decline to do so. The state legislature and future voters lose the power to enact wealth taxes or retroactive taxes without first amending the state Constitution.
The measure amends the California Constitution and cannot be changed or repealed by the legislature alone; it would require another voter-approved constitutional amendment.

flags.quote: "Retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" means pensions; retirement accounts including but not limited to 401 (k) accounts, 403(b) accounts, and all other individual retirement accounts; mutual funds; and all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including but not limited to financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, personal belongings, and other assets used to produce or collect income or savings for retirement or financial planning.
flags.note: The definition of personal savings is extremely broad, encompassing 'all personal property, whether tangible or intangible', which extends far beyond what is conventionally considered a retirement holding.

flags.quote: No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026 may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax that operates retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date of the state law or constitutional provision.
flags.note: The measure bundles a prohibition on retroactive taxes with a separate prohibition on taxing the ownership of wealth, personal property, and retirement savings.

flags.quote: The provisions of this Act are severable.
This Act shall take effect at the earliest possible date in accordance with Section 10 of Article II of the California Constitution. This Act shall become operative on the same day it takes effect.
flags.note: Specifies an immediate effective and operative date.

flags.quote: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 12500) of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code or any other law, the Attorney General shall appoint independent counsel
flags.note: Overrides existing state laws regarding the Attorney General's representation to mandate the appointment of independent counsel.
